newsitem.title: USA: No quick action seen on U.S. campaign funds reform.
newsitem.headline: No quick action seen on U.S. campaign funds reform.

text.p: As Congress probes those who solicited and wrote huge checks to pay for last year's political campaigns, questions remained whether real changes in campaign finance law will result.

Republicans and Democrats on the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee opened the long-awaited hearings with statements lauding the bipartisan nature, but quickly turned to note that abuses were commited by both.

Candace Nelson, director of American University's Campaign Management Institute, said these statements reinforced the view held by the public that the abuses being investigated were the normal way of doing business in political campaigns.
This, plus the lack of dramatic revelations so far at the hearings, point to no groundswell of public demand for finance reform, she said.
"Short of that, I don't see it," she said when asked if the reforms would move through Congress this year.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said on Thursday no action was scheduled on campaign finance legislation and would not be "until we find out what abuses occurred in last year's election."

The 1996 congressional and presidential elections were the most expensive on record, with more than $2 billion spent by candidates and political parties including $260 million in "soft money" -- contributions to political parties that are outside the strict limits on giving to candidates.
"Our major political parties were driven by an apparently unquenchable thirst for for cash," Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a Connecticut Democrat, said as Tuesday's hearing opened.

Brookings Institution analyst Thomas Mann, a proponent of campaign finance reform, said the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee's long-awaited hearings produced no bombshells concerning abuses which new proposed new laws would be designed to curb.
"The Republican strategy (in the first phase) is to focus on violations of existing laws," Mann said.

But he said the second phase will delve into "soft money" contributions and use of tax-exempt organisations for issue oriented campaigns and that new emphasis could provide momentum for reform legislation.
Central to the Senate probe is John Huang, who reportedly raised $3.4 million for the Democratic party, of which about half was deemed to come from legally questionable sources and was returned.

Soft money can be raised without limit and the checks go directly to the party organisations for so-called "party building" activities, and are not to be used for a particular candidate. However, the Federal Election Commission has taken a broad view of party building activities.

While Congress could curb soft money contributions, the limits would pose a particular problem for the heavily indebted Democratic party. Last week, show business contributors raised $2.7 million in one night for the Democrats at a New York theatre party attended by President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore. About 15 percent of it was designed to help retire the party's $14 million debt.

The Senate committee's first witness, Democratic National Committee fund-raiser Richard Sullivan, told the panel soft money should be restrained. "I strongly believe that the system of soft money leads to problems, especially the unlimited nature of it," he told the panel.
Sen. John McCain, the Arizona Republican who is one of two in his party to champion campaign changes, said he was optimistic the hearings would lead to action.
His bill, sponsored with Democrat Russell Feingold of Wisconsin, would shut down the soft money contributions.
Senate Democrats wrote Lott urging him to schedule a vote on the bill. "I'm always glad to get letters from them," Lott told reporters.
